name: DC BLOX Myrtle Beach Cable Landing Station

profile.reading: Per DC BLOX's own site, this Myrtle Beach, South Carolina cable landing station and data center sits at 1401 Howard Road and currently operates 40,000 square feet, designed for expansion up to 125,000 square feet, with 19 MW of power capacity committed and planned. The facility is built to withstand sustained hurricane winds of 170 mph using pre-cast construction, runs 2N power generation, UPS, and switchgear with indirect adiabatic and evaporative N+1 cooling, and holds Uptime Institute Tier III concurrently maintainable design certification plus SOC 2 Type II compliance. As a subsea cable landing station, the site can host up to 5 cables (3 announced as of the operator's own page) across 72 cable pairs, and connects via a high-capacity dark fiber route running from Lithia Springs, Georgia to Myrtle Beach, with links to Atlanta's internet exchanges; this positions the facility as an East Coast subsea gateway distinct from DC BLOX's inland Southeast colocation sites like Birmingham and Chattanooga, tracked elsewhere in this registry. DC BLOX operates a network of data centers across the Southeast United States; per the company's own data center map page, it operates 23 facilities totaling 2,780,376 square feet and 470 critical MW company-wide, a company-level aggregate this registry does not apply to this individual facility's own figures above. No year-opened date was located in sourcing reachable this session. No public ownership structure or investor detail specific to DC BLOX was located in sourcing reachable this session. DC BLOX positions itself as a regional Southeast US colocation and network fabric provider rather than a national hyperscale operator, and this Myrtle Beach site's subsea cable landing role gives the company a distinctive coastal gateway function alongside its inland colocation facilities in markets like Birmingham, Chattanooga, and Huntsville, a strategy distinct from the dense Northern Virginia or Silicon Valley clustering seen among many other operators tracked in this registry.

reading.body:
This cable landing station in Myrtle Beach operates 19 MW of IT capacity in 40,000 square feet of current technical space, with a design that allows expansion to 125,000 square feet. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, the current 19 MW represents roughly 475 racks, though the operator has not published what workload density it actually supports. The facility holds Uptime Institute Tier III concurrency maintenance certification and SOC 2 Type II compliance, qualifying it for critical workloads requiring continuous availability and regulated data handling.

The site's distinctive role is as a subsea cable gateway, with capacity for up to 5 subsea cables across 72 cable pairs, currently with 3 cables announced. It connects via dedicated dark fiber to Lithia Springs, Georgia and onward to Atlanta's internet exchanges, positioning it as an East Coast entry point for transoceanic data traffic rather than a landlocked colocation facility. This coastal gateway function sets it apart from DC BLOX's inland Southeast facilities.

In South Carolina, 14 data center facilities are mapped and 4 report published capacity totaling 6.6 MW. This Myrtle Beach site ranks fifth among those four published facilities in the state, though no comparison across the mapped 14 is possible from published data alone. DC BLOX operates 23 facilities across the Southeast totaling 470 MW company-wide, but this facility's own opening date and ownership structure are not published.
